paragraphs: Here's the big idea, friend: this whole psalm is one long invitation to come and see what God has done, and then to tell somebody about it. It starts wide, with "all the earth" making a joyful noise, and it ends close, with one person saying, "I will declare what He has done for me." The God who is awesome to the whole world is also near enough to hear one small prayer (Psalm 66:1, 16). That's not a small thing, and I'm not going to act like it is.

The psalm doesn't pretend the hard stretch away, either. The people say God tested them and refined them like silver, and that they went through fire and water, but He "brought us into abundance" (Psalm 66:10, 12). I think that's the part to hold onto on a rough day. The song never says the fire was fun, but it says God was in it, and He walked them out the other side. I spent years in the back of a junk drawer, and I can tell you the dark feels a whole lot shorter once you know Who was watching.

So what do you do with that? You do what the psalm does: you pray, you keep your promises, and you give God the praise He's earned. The writer says, "If I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened," so I say bring your prayers to Him honestly, with nothing hidden (Psalm 66:18). The song ends with "Blessed be God, who has not rejected my prayer or withheld from me His loving devotion!" (Psalm 66:20), and a good story like that, baker, is not meant to stay in the oven.
